phase1.intro:
Okay — first real program. Let's actually build something.

Where do you want to start?

topics.buttonText: Where does my code actually live?
dialogue: Every Java program lives inside a [[term:class]] — remember, that's the blueprint idea from lesson one. Here, the blueprint is named `HelloWorld`.
[[warn:The class name has to match the filename exactly]] — capital letters and all. This blueprint has to live in a file called `HelloWorld.java`.

stickyNote.flavor: 📁 the blueprint's name IS the file's name
stickyNote.definition: A public class's name must exactly match its .java filename, including capitalization.

topics.buttonText: How does Java know where to start?
dialogue: Inside that blueprint, Java needs one very specific starting point: `public static void main(String[] args)`. Think of `main` as the front door.
[[key:This is the exact line Java looks for when it decides where to start running your program]]. Get the spelling or capitalization even slightly wrong, and Java won't find a way in.

stickyNote.flavor: 🚪 the front door Java always looks for
stickyNote.definition: public static void main(String[] args) is the required entry point every runnable Java program starts from.

topics.buttonText: How do I actually print something?
dialogue: Once we're inside `main`, the actual work is one line: `System.out.println("Hello, World!")`. `System.out` is your direct line to the console.
[[term:println]] prints your text and then moves to a new line, ready for whatever prints next.

stickyNote.flavor: 📣 your direct line to the console
stickyNote.definition: Prints the given text to the console, then moves to a new line so the next output starts fresh.

topics.buttonText: What rules should I lock in early?
dialogue: A couple of things to lock in now, because they'll matter every single lesson from here. Java is [[warn:case-sensitive]] — `String` and `string` are not the same thing, ever.
And every single statement ends with a semicolon `;`. Miss one, and the compiler stops cold — which, conveniently, is exactly what we're about to watch happen next.

stickyNote.flavor: ⚠️ the two rules that break code the most
stickyNote.definition: Java is case-sensitive (String ≠ string), and every statement must end with a semicolon.

phase1.openingDialogue: Ah, the classic! Let me show you your very first Java program~ ✨

phase2.errorMessage:
HelloWorld.java:3: error: ';' expected
        System.out.println("Hello, World!")
                                             ^
1 error
phase2.explanation:
See the missing `;` after the very last thing on line 3? [[warn:every statement needs one]] — no exceptions, not even the last line inside a method. Look closely at the error message: the compiler even points a `^` right at the exact spot it expected the semicolon to be.

This is genuinely the single most common mistake anyone makes starting out. [[key:When the compiler complains about a missing semicolon, it usually points at the END of the broken line, not somewhere further down]] — so always check the line right where that `^` lands first.

phase3.openingDialogue: Your turn! Let's see what you've got~ 💪

mcq.question:
Which of these is a valid Java entry point?

A) public void main(String[] args)
B) public static void main(String[] args)
C) static void Main(string[] args)
D) public static int main(String args)

phase4.selfChallenge:
Write a Java program that prints "Hello, Java-chan!" to the console.

Requirements:
• Use a class named HelloJava
• Use the correct main method signature
• Print exactly: Hello, Java-chan!

phase5.trivia: [[fun:Fun fact]]: "Hello, World!" as the very first program in a new language is a tradition way older than Java. It traces back to a 1978 C programming book by Brian Kernighan and Dennis Ritchie — Java (1995) didn't invent the tradition, it just kept it going. Pretty much every language you'll ever learn will have you write this exact same program first.
phase5.openingDialogue: Before you move on — one more thing~

hoverNotes.HelloWorld: This is the example class name for this lesson — the file must be named HelloWorld.java to match it exactly.
